group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
A 66-year-old man arrived to the emergency department by private automobile in the late morning after three days of progressively wetter cough, right-sided pleuritic chest discomfort, and new dyspnea climbing the single flight of stairs to the bedroom of his split-level home. He reports intermittent shaking chills that had him layering extra blankets overnight and an axillary temperature at home reaching 38 °C earlier today, but he declined antipyretics, inhalers, or any rescue medications so that the clinical team could evaluate an unaltered presentation. His partner confirms that the drive was uneventful and that he conversed normally, correctly reciting the date and the route they planned to take. Past health history is notable for a stage II left-sided colonic adenocarcinoma resected two years ago followed by six months of adjuvant capecitabine; surveillance colonoscopy six months earlier and recent carcinoembryonic antigen levels have been unremarkable, and he has no current weight loss or night sweats. In addition, he follows cardiology for long-standing ischemic systolic dysfunction diagnosed after an anterior wall myocardial infarction seven years ago; the most recent outpatient echocardiogram three months prior documented a left-ventricular ejection fraction of 35 % with mild biatrial enlargement and trace mitral regurgitation. Home medications taken yesterday morning include carvedilol 25 mg twice daily, lisinopril 5 mg daily, low-dose furosemide 20 mg each morning, low-dose aspirin, rosuvastatin, and a daily multivitamin. He monitors his weight each day and had not noticed any sudden gain preceding this illness. There is no chronic kidney impairment, his last recorded serum creatinine being 1.0 mg/dL at a clinic visit six weeks ago, and he has never required dialysis. He denies chronic liver problems, tuberculosis, or connective-tissue disease. Immunizations are up to date, including both pneumococcal formulations and last season’s influenza vaccine. He quit a 30-pack-year cigarette habit a decade earlier, drinks red wine with dinner twice weekly, and denies illicit drug use. Upon arrival he sat upright on the stretcher, speaking in full sentences with mild breaks for breath, appearing uncomfortable but alert and oriented to person, place, time, and circumstance. Skin was warm and lightly diaphoretic; mucous membranes were slightly dry with brisk capillary refill. Pre-intervention vital signs measured by triage nursing staff on room air at this sea-level facility were: oral temperature 38.0 °C, regular pulse 104 beats min⁻¹ confirmed with three-lead telemetry, non-invasive blood pressure 109/64 mm Hg verified manually, respiratory rate 26 breaths min⁻¹ with moderate use of intercostal muscles, and fingertip pulse oximetry fluctuating between 90 % and 92 % while breathing ambient air. Jugular venous distention was estimated at 4 cm above the sternal angle while the patient reclined at 45°, consistent with his chronic cardiology baseline, and trace bilateral ankle edema was present. Cardiac auscultation revealed a soft S3 in addition to normal S1 and S2 without new murmurs. Lung examination showed decreased breath sounds and stony dullness to percussion at the right posterior base with fine inspiratory crackles just superior to that area; the left lung had scattered coarse crackles in the lower field but remained resonant overall, and no wheezes were appreciated. The abdomen was soft, nontender, with normoactive bowel sounds, and the post-surgical midline scar from prior colectomy was well healed. A focused neurologic screen demonstrated equal, reactive pupils, intact extra-ocular movements, fluent speech, and 5/5 strength in all extremities. Capillary blood glucose obtained before phlebotomy registered 112 mg dL⁻¹. Venous blood drawn within ten minutes of arrival—prior to any intravenous fluid, oxygen supplementation, or medications save for minimal heparinized saline used to lock the catheter—returned a basic metabolic panel of sodium 133 mEq L⁻¹, potassium 4.1 mEq L⁻¹, chloride 101 mEq L⁻¹, bicarbonate 24 mEq L⁻¹, blood urea nitrogen 23 mg dL⁻¹, and creatinine 1.0 mg dL⁻¹. Complete blood count showed leukocytosis to 14.0 × 10⁹ L⁻¹ with 88 % neutrophils, hematocrit 37 %, hemoglobin 12.4 g dL⁻¹, and platelets 245 × 10⁹ L⁻¹. An arterial sample taken from the right radial artery while the patient remained on room air demonstrated pH 7.38, PaCO₂ 34 mm Hg, PaO₂ 70 mm Hg, and calculated bicarbonate 20 mEq L⁻¹, reflecting mild hypoxemia with an acid–base status near physiologic. Serum lactate measured 1.7 mmol L⁻¹. Twelve-lead electrocardiography displayed sinus tachycardia at 106 beats min⁻¹ with old anterior Q waves and nonspecific T-wave flattening unchanged from previous tracings. A portable postero-anterior chest radiograph obtained before any therapy revealed a moderate right-sided fluid collection layering above the diaphragm with a concave meniscus sign, obscuring the costophrenic angle, along with a patchy consolidation of the adjacent right lower lobe; the cardiac silhouette was borderline enlarged, and pulmonary vasculature appeared mildly cephalized compared with prior imaging. Two sets of peripheral blood cultures, an expectorated sputum specimen for Gram stain and culture, urinary antigens for Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella, and a respiratory viral PCR panel were dispatched prior to antibiotics or diuretics. At the instant this note is dictated the patient has received no antipyretics, bronchodilators, supplemental oxygen, intravenous crystalloids, vasopressors, or other medications, so every physiologic observation, laboratory value, and imaging finding recorded above reflects his untreated presentation.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) adds demographic, comorbidity, examination, laboratory, and imaging points from the untreated presentation.
- Demographics: A man starts with his age in years = 66. He lives at home, so nursing-home residence adds 0.
- Comorbidities: Colon cancer treated within the past five years = +30 despite negative surveillance. Chronic systolic heart failure (LVEF 35%) = +10. No liver, cerebrovascular, or chronic renal disease is documented = 0 each.
- Examination: He is oriented (no altered mental status), RR 26 is below 30/min, systolic BP 109 is not below 90 mmHg, temperature 38.0°C is neither below 35°C nor at least 40°C, and pulse 104 is below 125/min = 0 each.
- Tests: pH 7.38 is not below 7.35; BUN 23 is below 30 mg/dL; sodium 133 is not below 130 mEq/L; glucose 112 is below 250 mg/dL; hematocrit 37% is not below 30% = 0 each. Room-air PaO₂ 70 mmHg and saturation 90–92% do not meet the hypoxemia threshold (PaO₂ <60 mmHg or saturation <90%) = 0.
- Imaging: Right pleural effusion = +10.
Total = 66 + 30 + 10 + 10 = 116.
Final answer: 116
